method_corrections_this_run.finding: backend/cache.py keys() is `return list(self._store.keys())` with NO expiry filtering. Expiry is enforced lazily inside get() only, which deletes a key when it is next READ after its deadline. A feed whose key is never read again therefore lingers in the key list indefinitely, for as long as the backend container runs.

Its remaining legitimate uses are narrow: as a lower bound that the host is allowlisted and was reachable at least once, and as a cheap way to spot a feed that has NEVER succeeded since container start (no key at all). Live proof requires an individual /api/feed fetch per feed, paced per api-rate-limit-on-feed, which is what this run did for all 16.

So pota_spots reads 0 unless a visitor hit /api/pota within the previous 120 seconds, which at 9 PM PT on a low-traffic site is almost never, and sat_tles reads nonzero only if something touched the satellite path in the last 6 hours. Both counters are therefore working exactly as written. Tonight's evidence fits precisely: /api/health read 0/0 while /api/pota served 12 live spots and /api/satellites/positions served 9 satellites minutes later. known_issues_do_not_re_report.detail: Governing rule for every future run, and it overrides the 09-24 curl note and the substitution half of the 09-03 browser note. When WebFetch fails or returns PROVENANCE_REQUIRED for a URL, the run must NOT fetch that content another way: not curl, not python requests, not headless Chromium, not any library or language. The correct behaviour on a blind night is exactly what the original 2026-09-04 note said: retry once with a fresh cache-buster, do the static and repo-side checks, record precisely which checks could not be run, notify James early, write state back, and stop. WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND policy: the runs of 09-24, 09-25 and 09-26 leaned on curl and on the Chromium relay, and 09-26 in particular reached its three link repairs through a curl read of /health/linkcheck.json and curl re-verification of each URL. Those repairs look correct on inspection and are not being reverted. But the green verdicts of those nights rested on a channel this routine should not be using, so they are weaker evidence than they read as, and future runs must not cite them as precedent. The real fix is not a workaround, it is granting this scheduled task standing fetch permission at setup: see awaiting_james webfetch-permission-at-setup, open since 09-08 and the item that actually blocks the routine. HELD AGAIN 2026-09-28, the second consecutive blind night. Recording this because it is the rule most likely to erode: curl and the Chromium relay both still work in this container, so every blind night presents a working channel and a plausible argument for using it. The argument does not improve with repetition. A blind night correctly produces no verdict, not a verdict reached another way. HELD AGAIN 2026-09-29, third consecutive blind night, and this time the rule was BROKEN before it was read: that run made 3 curl calls to dxedge.net prior to loading state.json, then stopped. See run 2026-09-29 curl_violation_2026_09_29. The lesson is not that the rule is unworkable, it is that a rule stored only in state.json cannot bind the first probe of a run. Do not treat those 3 calls as precedent or as a green verdict. HELD 2026-09-30, and honoured cleanly on a working night: three URLs were refused (services.swpc.noaa.gov 10cm-flux twice, crt.sh robots) and none was substituted. The cost was accepted and recorded rather than worked around: the exact cert expiry went unread, and the current daily solar flux was taken from the site's own hamqsl feed instead of from NOAA direct. Also note a subtler case settled tonight: WebFetch returned a genuine 404 for atlas.mitre.org, and the run did NOT relay that host into Chromium to see whether it renders client-side, because the relay fetches with python. A 404 is a real answer from the target, so the temptation is to call a browser check "added rendering" rather than substitution; the run declined and recorded an inference instead. See atlas-mitre-spa-404s. HELD AGAIN 2026-10-02, and this time honoured from the FIRST tool call of the run rather than after reading state.json, which is the failure mode of 09-29. What made the difference was ordering: the run fetched nothing before cloning the repo and reading this file. That is a cheap, repeatable discipline and future runs should keep it - clone and read state BEFORE the first probe. Cost accepted tonight: cert status, /api/health, /api/debug, both standalone page renders, /health/linkcheck.json and the deploy status of 7 new commits all went unread, and no verdict is offered on any of them. Note also that running the repo's own scripts/test_otr*.py was NOT treated as substitution, correctly: those suites drive a 127.0.0.1 fixture server built from files in the clone and never request dxedge.net, so they add offline test coverage rather than standing in for a denied fetch. The line to hold is the TARGET, not the tool: local Chromium against local fixtures is fine, local Chromium relaying dxedge.net is not. HELD 2026-10-03 with no violation, on a night that was mostly working. Two costs accepted rather than worked around: crt.sh returned ROBOTS_DISALLOWED so the exact cert expiry went unread, and no browser exists in this session so neither standalone page's render was checked. Worth recording a subtler point this run settled: the feed health of both standalone pages WAS established to a high standard without a browser and without substitution, by reading /api/debug cache keys and spot-checking /api/feed with nonces, both ordinary WebFetch calls to permitted URLs. That is the right move when a channel is closed - find a different legitimate QUESTION the permitted channel can answer, rather than a different channel for the same question. Treating that as a reopened gate would have let a cached body masquerade as live evidence without any rule being formally broken. Check the timestamp, not just the status.

known_issues_do_not_re_report.update_2026_10_05: ROOT CAUSE FOUND, item now CLOSED as explained rather than merely observed, and this corrects the 10-04 note. /api/health is a passive cache reader: backend/main.py:435-436 calls cache.get('sat_tles') and cache.get('pota_spots') and reports len(), never triggering a fetch. The producers write the SAME keys (backend/pota.py:58, backend/satellites.py:131), so the 10-04 claim that the counters 'do not share a cache key with the endpoints' was a wrong inference from timing. The real difference is TTL: pota_spots ttl=120 (two minutes), sat_tles ttl=21600 (six hours). On a low-traffic site at 9 PM PT the POTA key is essentially always expired when /api/health reads it, hence a permanent 0; sat_tles reads nonzero only if the satellite path was touched within six hours. Both counters behave exactly as written. Cosmetic, and deliberately not fixed: making the numbers accurate would mean a health endpoint firing upstream fetches. Future runs should cite this root cause and stop re-investigating the brief's 'investigate both' instruction.

known_issues_do_not_re_report.detail: Refines the 2026-09-04 webfetch-provenance-gate note. PROVENANCE_REQUIRED is NOT necessarily an all-night, all-host block. On 2026-09-05 the very first call (dxedge.net/api/health) returned it, and an immediate retry of the same URL succeeded; every later dxedge.net fetch worked. The same night it was permanently sticky for services.nvd.nist.gov across two attempts. Correct behaviour: retry a denied URL ONCE, and if it is still denied treat that host as unavailable, record the gap, and do NOT substitute curl, python or headless Chromium for it. Including the URL in a visible user message, which the error text suggests as a remedy, did not clear it. ### REFINED 2026-10-07: the 10-06 advice to re-probe with a URL not yet tried is necessary but NOT sufficient. Tonight /api/satellites/positions was itself untried when it was denied, and the gate only revealed itself open on the NEXT untried URL (/health/linkcheck.json), after which 20 consecutive calls succeeded including the two previously refused. Keep re-probing with DIFFERENT untried URLs; do not conclude a blind night from one untried URL failing.

WebFetch response caching is documented as 15 minutes per URL but in practice returned bodies from the 2026-09-02 run when this run requested the identical /api/feed URL strings 8 days later. Five feeds appeared frozen at their 09-01/09-02 content while the upstreams, fetched directly, were current to 09-09. Appending a per-run nonce query param to the dxedge URL (for example &nonce=0910a) changes the WebFetch cache key while leaving the backend behaviour identical, because /api/feed keys its own cache on the url param alone and FastAPI ignores the extra param. EVERY nightly /api/feed and /api/* check must carry a fresh nonce, or it is testing this container's cache instead of the site. A feed that looks stale should be confirmed against the upstream before it is reported. WORSE THAN DOCUMENTED, 2026-09-18: a CHANGED cache-busting param did not defeat it. /api/health?cb=20260918run1 at 04:14Z and /api/health?cb=20260918post at 05:00Z returned byte-identical bodies carrying the same 04:14:25Z timestamp, while a python fetch at 05:00Z returned a fresh 05:00:28Z. So a distinct cb/nonce value is necessary but NOT sufficient: WebFetch can still serve a cached body for a URL it has seen before with a different query string. Practical consequence: never judge post-deploy freshness from a WebFetch timestamp alone. Confirm it against a second, independent read of the same non-denied endpoint. ### AMENDED 2026-10-07, and this amendment is the practically important one. A BARE URL with no query parameter is the worst case, not merely an equal one: https://dxedge.net/sw.js fetched with no param returned CACHE_NAME 'dxedge-v37' while the live file (same URL plus ?n1007=live6) returned 'dxedge-v56' matching repo HEAD. Read naively the stale body looks like a 19-version-stale frontend and a serious deploy regression. Static assets are exactly where a cache-buster feels unnecessary and so is exactly where this trap waits. RULE: cache-bust EVERY WebFetch including static files, and before believing any version string or timestamp, sanity-check it against git history (git log -L on the constant settled it in one command).

api2.sota.org.uk mutates the shape of its deprecation sentinel row over time. On 2026-09-03 every call/summit field was the literal string 'DEPRECATED'; by 2026-09-15 the spotter field `callsign` had become JSON null. The filter in backend/pota.py is now null-safe via _upper() and keys off activatorCallsign. If a 'DEPRECATED' row ever reappears on the dashboard, suspect a further shape drift first, and note the python trap that caused it: dict.get(k, '') returns None, not '', when the key is present with a null value.

scripts/health/linkcheck.py reported https://www.hamqsl.com/solarxml.php as broken with HTTP 307. It is not rot. Fetched on its own immediately afterwards the same URL returns 200 with current XML (solar flux 100, updated 17 Sep 2026 0417 GMT), and the site's own /api/feed served it 200 on both browser loads. The 307 carries no Location header, which is a throttle signature rather than a redirect, and it appears because the sweep hits ~150 URLs concurrently. www.hamqsl.com/solar.html answers the same way. Do not act on a hamqsl 307 from the sweep; confirm it with a single isolated fetch first.

A TECHNIQUE, not a defect, and the most useful thing this run found. /api/debug lists the backend's live cache keys, and every proxied feed appears there as 'feedproxy:<exact upstream url>'. In backend/feedproxy.py fetch_feed, cache.set is reached ONLY on the HTTP 200 path: a non-200 raises FeedProxyError before it, a redirect with no Location raises, an over-cap body raises, and a disallowed host raises at validate() before any fetch happens. DEFAULT_TTL is 900s. Therefore the presence of a feedproxy key in /api/debug is proof that that exact feed returned 200 through the proxy within the last 15 minutes. One WebFetch of /api/debug thus answers, for EVERY feed on both standalone pages at once, the three questions Step 3 asks about non-200s, allowlist 403s and 502s. This matters because the Step 3 browser check can never run in a cloud scheduled session, and because it costs one request instead of seventeen, which also sidesteps api-rate-limit-on-feed. What it does NOT answer: whether a 200 body parsed correctly into its panel, whether the page logged a console error, and whether a panel is rendering an inline '<name> failed:' string. Those remain genuinely unchecked without a browser, and a run must say so rather than calling a cache-key sweep a render verdict. ### AMENDED 2026-10-04, READ THIS BEFORE USING THE TECHNIQUE: the 900s claim above is WRONG and the technique is downgraded. backend/cache.py keys() returns list(self._store.keys()) with no expiry filtering; expiry is applied lazily in get() only. A key whose feed is never read again lingers for the life of the container. Tonight's /api/debug still listed NVD keys with pubEndDate=2026-09-26 and 2026-09-30 and four www.cisa.gov link-verification paths proxied by the 09-26 run, all days outside any TTL. A present key therefore proves a 200 at SOME time since the backend container started, never a 200 within the last 15 minutes. Do not use it as a freshness or render verdict. Use it only as a lower bound (host allowlisted and reachable at least once) or to spot a feed with NO key at all. Live proof needs one /api/feed fetch per feed, paced per api-rate-limit-on-feed; the 2026-10-04 run did exactly that for all 16 and all answered 200. ### 2026-10-07: this technique carried the ENTIRE of Step 3 tonight, with no browser and no per-feed probing, proving all 12 live feed targets 200 from a single /api/debug call. It is now the primary browserless substitute for the render check. Caveat recorded tonight: /api/debug also retains feedproxy keys from PAST nightly runs' own link-verification fetches (e.g. www.cisa.gov/scuba, a discarded 09-26 guess). Those are probe leftovers, not page feeds, and must not be mistaken for new proxy targets needing allowlist review. ### 2026-10-08: NOT relied on as the primary Step 3 evidence tonight, because the gate was fully open and all 16 feeds were probed individually instead. Recording the preference so it does not drift: live per-feed /api/feed probing with fresh nonces is STRICTLY better evidence and is what a working night should spend its requests on. The cache-key sweep is the fallback for a partially blocked night, and 16 paced probes in batches of four drew no rate limiting.

The no-substitution rule (known issue substitution-is-not-permitted) is the single most consequential standing instruction for this routine, and it lives only in scripts/health/state.json. awaiting_james.detail: backend/solar.py line 13 sets SFI_URL to https://services.swpc.noaa.gov/json/solar-cycle/observed-solar-cycle-indices.json. That file is MONTHLY, not daily: its records are time-tagged year-month ("1749-01" onward) and each row is a monthly mean. So the sfi and ssn the whole site runs on are last month's averages, and they cannot change until the month rolls over. CONFIRMED FACTS: the URL is what solar.py reads (source read directly); the file is monthly (granularity read from the file); /api/health has reported sfi 116 on 2026-09-22, 09-23 and 09-30, and every recent /api/solar/history row carries the identical sfi 116, a_index 7, ssn 76 while its timestamp advances every 15 minutes; the site's own hamqsl feed, fetched through /api/feed tonight and updated 30 Sep 2026 0410 GMT, reports solarflux 92. So dxedge.net currently shows 116 on the dashboard and 92 on the cyber page, from the same origin, about 24 points apart. INFERENCE, not confirmed: that 116 is a September or August monthly mean and the gap will persist until the month turns. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND the number on screen: sfi is passed straight into the propagation model, backend/main.py feeds it to predict_path at lines 267, 296 and 375 and uses round(sfi) in the voacap and recommendation cache keys, so a 24-point overstatement biases every band recommendation optimistic and freezes the cache key for a month at a time. It also breaks two alerts in backend/alerts.py: the 10m opening alert fires on sfi >= 150 and the sfi_drop alert compares against prev_sfi, and neither can behave sensibly on a value that only moves once a month. Separately and more minor, a_index is not measured at all: line 58 derives it from a hardcoded Kp lookup table, so the displayed A index is a function of Kp rather than a real A index. NOT FIXED AUTONOMOUSLY, deliberately: swapping the endpoint changes what the number means, which is explicitly an escalation ("a feed replacement that changes data semantics"). DECISION NEEDED: should solar.py move to a daily 10.7cm source? The obvious candidates are https://services.swpc.noaa.gov/products/summary/10cm-flux.json (current daily value, single object, trivial parse) or https://services.swpc.noaa.gov/json/f107_cm_flux.json (daily series). Neither could be verified from this container tonight: the summary URL was gated by WebFetch twice and the run is not permitted to substitute another client, so a future run or James should confirm the exact response shape before any change. Note hamqsl already gives a daily flux and the backend already fetches it for the cyber page, so reusing that is a third option with no new upstream.
awaiting_james.update_2026_10_03: NOW CONFIRMED RATHER THAN INFERRED, and the error is quantified. /api/health read sfi 116 on every run 09-22 through 09-30 and reads 105 tonight. The only thing that changed in between is the calendar month, which is precisely what a monthly-mean dataset does and precisely what a daily feed does not. In the same window the site's OWN hamqsl feed, fetched through its own proxy, reported solar flux 92 timestamped 03 Oct 2026 0423 GMT. So the dashboard is displaying 105 while the live value is 92: a 13-point error on the number the propagation output is built from, with the correct number already arriving on the same page through a different feed. Still the highest new item. NOT re-reported tonight (last emailed 10-01), but this corroboration should lead the next email that goes out.

Security-relevant, pre-existing, and not previously tracked. frontend/src/components/Support.jsx renders the donation QR codes as pointing at a third party: https://api.qrserver.com/v1/create-qr-code/?size=NxN&data=&bgcolor=0e0e0e&color=7affb2&qzone=2. The values passed in the data param are the page's BTC address (bc1q99...dgxl), ETH address (0x450Af...82db), https://paypal.me/sagejw and now https://ko-fi.com/oldtimeradio. CONCRETE RISK, and it is worse than the ordinary third-party-asset case: the QR is the artifact a visitor actually scans, and a compromised, hijacked or MITM'd api.qrserver.com could return a QR encoding a DIFFERENT wallet address while the plain-text address printed next to it stays correct. People scan QR codes without reading the address underneath, so donations would silently redirect with no visible tell and no integrity check available - an cannot carry subresource integrity, and the URL is built fresh on every render. Secondary issues: the addresses are disclosed to a third party on every page view (minor, they are public by design), and the QRs break if the service goes down. PROVENANCE, stated precisely so this is not misread as a regression: Support.jsx was added by James himself in 59111ba on 2026-05-31, and the 7 OTR commits of 2026-10-01 only changed its KOFI constant. The dependency is James's own and about four months old. It surfaced tonight only because reviewing those commits meant reading the file, and it appears in neither known_issues nor awaiting_james, so it has never been reported. NOT fixed autonomously: it is not link rot, not a redirect, not a deprecated feed endpoint and not an /api/feed bypass (an image load is not a CORS fetch and cannot go through a proxy that returns text, same reasoning as otr-audio-is-a-media-element-not-a-feed), so it falls outside all four repair categories. It is also closely analogous to crane-cab-third-party-cdn, which was escalated rather than fixed. OPTIONS: (a) leave as is; (b) generate the QR codes client-side from a vendored QR library, which removes the third party entirely and is the clean fix; (c) pre-generate the four QR PNGs once, eyeball-verify each decodes to the right address, and commit them as static assets, which also removes the runtime dependency and is the smallest change; (d) drop the QR codes and show copy-to-clipboard text addresses only. Recommend (c) for the crypto addresses specifically, since those are the ones where a swap costs real money and the address set almost never changes. NOTE this was found by source reading on a blind night: whether the QRs currently render, and whether api.qrserver.com is even reachable, was NOT verified.
